newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler calls on labour to aid competitive drive.
newsitem.headline: Daimler calls on labour to aid competitive drive.

text.p: Juergen Schrempp, chairman of German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, on Thursday called on workers to tone down recent tough talk and save their jobs by helping industry become more competitive.

In a speech presented to a German think-tank, Schrempp suggested that Daimler, Germany's largest company, was ready to meet labour half-way in on-going fights over sick pay and other benefits, but that labour costs must be reduced.
"The art of company management is to satisfy the demands of shareholders, workers and customers. And this can be accomplished only by consensus, not by conflict," Schrempp said.
Highlights of the speech were made available to reporters.

Daimler, as much as any firm in Germany, has been the target of union criticism after it was among the first German firms to announce in September it would take advantage of a new German law allowing sick pay to be reduced from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
The company has been hit wild-cat strikes which have delayed production of some of its best-selling cars and cost it millions of marks in production.
Schrempp said the cuts were needed to make Daimler more internationally competitive and preserve German jobs.

"No board wants to cut the pay of man sick in bed, but if we succeed in reducing the sick quota on Monday and Friday, will ensure jobs and help the company to be more internationally competitive," Schrempp said.
Daimler executives have been especially critical of employees phoning in sick on those days, suggesting workers were taking advantage of generous sick benefits to enjoy frequent long weekends.
"Companies must not be overly burdened, otherwise they will not be able to fulfil their basic tasks," he said.
Schrempp's remarks come as German labour unions continued to bluster against industry efforts to slash benefits.

German trade unions lashed out on Wednesday against "unfettered capitalism" in Germany. "I don't want an unfettered market economy and an authoritarian, anti-society republic," said Dieter Schulte, chairman of the DGB German Federation of Trade Unions.
